title: "Chicago Blazes. The alarm from Box No. 98 at 4:45 o'clock yesterday afternoon was caused by an overheated stove in the two-story brick barn in the rear of No. 1834 Prairie avenue, owned and occupied by W. F. Storey. Damage $400. Fully insured."
creator: Chicago Daily Tribune ('Chicago Blazes' fire column)
collection: The Chicago Daily Tribune, Jan. 22, 1883 (vol. 42), page index 1
found_via: IA full-text search '"Storey" "1834 Prairie"' (owner-name pass); item read on the page image (IIIF crop) — the OCR interleaves columns
notes: Answers part of the 1834 Storey lead and adds an outbuilding: in January 1883 a TWO-STOREY BRICK BARN stood at the rear (alley) of 1834 Prairie, and Wilbur F. Storey (proprietor of the Chicago Times) was living in the house; a stove fire did $400 damage, 'fully insured'. The paper says 'owned and occupied by W. F. Storey', but the Storey will-contest reporting (Tribune 20 Jan 1886, npo-1834-tribune-1886-01-20-storey-letters-jones-house) states the house belonged to Fernando Jones and Storey was his tenant — read 'owned' here as loose wording. Bearing on 1904: the 1834 lot carried a two-storey brick barn by 1883 (it is the brick stable square on the Robinson 1886 plate and should be modelled at the alley in 1904 unless later evidence removes it). It also shows the house pre-dates 1883, consistent with the 1866–67 Van Osdel construction (dw-indchi-1891-v1-1867-van-osdel-jones) rather than a post-1871 date.

title: Storey will contest: "In a letter of Nov. 14, 1881, Mr. Storey abuses Fernando Jones and all his people… The Prairie avenue house he lived in belonged to Jones…"
creator: Chicago Daily Tribune (report of the Wilbur F. Storey will case, Probate Court)
collection: The Chicago Daily Tribune, Jan. 20, 1886 (vol. 46), page index 1
found_via: IA full-text search '"Fernando Jones" "Storey" Prairie' (owner-name pass); passage read on the page image (IIIF crop)
notes: Settles who owned 1834 while Storey lived there: "In a letter of Nov. 14, 1881, Mr. Storey abuses Fernando Jones and all his people—'damn them,' etc. The Prairie avenue house he lived in belonged to Jones, and he had an idea that there was sewer-gas there, and that it had poisoned him, and wanted A. S. Trude to sue him for a million dollar damages and to hurry the matter up." So the house at 1834 was Fernando Jones's property and Storey was renting it by Nov. 1881 (he died there on 27 Oct 1884; funeral from the house). With the 1883 barn-fire item this answers the WORKLOG lead: Storey's residence does NOT bear on a later construction date — the house is Jones's 1866–67 Van Osdel building, let to Storey c.1881–84; the Joneses returned after Storey's death, and the library's '1886 mansard addition' falls after they moved back. The 1904 house is therefore the Jones house as enlarged in 1886. No architectural description in the passage.

Whether it still stood, empty or let, in 1904 is not settled by any item found — the demolition window is now late 1902 to 1911, and the library's 'uncertain; likely absent' should stay open rather than be reversed.
